text: Up to now you've explored data in Python. Power BI is the other tool many analysts and stakeholders live in, and you'll often need to hand findings to people who'd rather click a report than read a notebook. This lesson covers the plumbing: bringing data in from SQL Server and from Python.

In Power BI Desktop, choose Get data, then SQL Server database. You'll pick Import or DirectQuery. Import copies the data into the file, fast and full-featured, but it's a snapshot until refreshed. DirectQuery leaves data in the source and queries it live, so it stays current, but it's slower with more restrictions.

Under Advanced options there's a SQL statement box. Paste a query there and the heavy filtering and aggregation happen in the database, loading only a small result. Since you already write SQL, this is often the cleanest route: shape the data where it lives, load a small table.

To enable Python, install it locally plus pandas and matplotlib, then go to File, Options and settings, Options, Python scripting, and point Power BI at your Python home directory. Microsoft recommends the official python-dot-org distribution, since environments needing an extra activation step, like Conda, might fail to run.

Choose Get data, Other, Python script, paste your script, and click OK. Power BI runs it, and every pandas data frame the script creates appears as a table in the Navigator. On our illustrative customer file, this produced a by-region table matching the churn rates from earlier lessons exactly.

You can also run Python inside Power Query itself. On the Transform tab, select Run Python script; the loaded table arrives as a data frame named dataset. Running the outlier flag from an earlier lesson against it flags the same nineteen rows.

Mind the limits: scripts time out past thirty minutes, nested tables aren't supported, and data sources in a Python query need their privacy level set to public. For anything a team depends on daily, do the heavy work upstream in SQL and load the result. Next: building exploratory reports.
